claim: Cyclin B1 continues to be degraded during anaphase in Drosophila S2 cells
source: In agreement with previous reports (Clute and Pines, 1999; Huang and Raff, 1999), cytoplasmic Cyclin B1-GFP levels decreased abruptly at the metaphase-anaphase transition (Figure 1a,c). However, in contrast to what has been observed in Drosophila embryos (Huang and Raff, 1999), the centrosomal pool of Cyclin B1 in S2 cells was the most resistant to degradation and persisted well after anaphase onset, becoming undetectable only ~1 min before DNA decondensation (Figure 1a,c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,a' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,d,e and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data showing Cyclin B1-GFP levels during anaphase in S2 cells (Figure 1a,c) and quantification showing persistence of centrosomal Cyclin B1 until ~1 min before DNA decondensation

claim: Complete Cyclin B1 disappearance from centrosomes during anaphase strongly correlates with mitotic exit in Drosophila S2 cells
source: Indeed, complete Cyclin B1 disappearance from centrosomes during anaphase strongly correlated with mitotic exit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2f demonstrating statistical relationship between Cyclin B1 disappearance and anaphase duration

claim: Cyclin B1 continues to be degraded during anaphase in human HeLa and hTERT-RPE1 cells
source: To extend the significance of these observations, we monitored endogenously tagged Cyclin B1-Venus levels in human HeLa and hTERT-RPE1 cells (Collin et al., 2013) throughout mitosis and found that it also continues to be degraded during anaphase (Figure 1b,c and Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,c and Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data of endogenously tagged Cyclin B1-Venus in human cells showing continued degradation during anaphase

claim: Cyclin B1 continues to be degraded during anaphase in primary adult Drosophila follicular epithelium cells
source: The physiological relevance of these findings was confirmed in primary adult Drosophila follicular epithelium cells (ex vivo) expressing endogenously tagged Cyclin B1-GFP (Figure 1d,e and Video 4)
evidence: Supported by live imaging data from primary Drosophila follicular epithelium cells showing Cyclin B1-GFP degradation during anaphase

claim: Cyclin B1 continues to be degraded during meiosis II in mouse oocytes
source: and after injection of Cyclin B1-mCherry mRNA in mouse oocytes undergoing meiosis II, when chromosomal division is similar to mitosis (Figure 1f,f', g).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data from mouse oocytes injected with Cyclin B1-mCherry mRNA showing degradation during meiosis II

claim: Cyclin B1 disappearance is a strong predictor of mitotic exit in metazoans
source: Thus, Cyclin B1 continues to be degraded during anaphase in Drosophila, mouse and human cells, including primary tissues, and its disappearance is a strong predictor of mitotic exit.
evidence: Inference based on correlation data from multiple species and cell types showing relationship between Cyclin B1 disappearance and mitotic exit timing

claim: Acute Cdk1 inhibition at anaphase onset accelerates nuclear envelope reformation in Drosophila S2 cells
source: To investigate the functional relevance of an anaphase Cyclin B1 pool we acutely inhibited Cdk1 activity at anaphase onset with RO-3306 (Vassilev et al., 2006) and found that it accelerated NER in S2 cells (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced anaphase duration after RO-3306 treatment at anaphase onset (Figure 2a-d)

claim: Expression of non-degradable Cyclin B1 prevents normal spindle elongation and induces an extensive delay in anaphase
source: In contrast, expression of non-degradable Cyclin B1 or Cyclin B3 prevented normal spindle elongation and induced an extensive delay in anaphase, in agreement with previous works (Afonso et al., 2014; Parry and O'Farrell, 2001; Potapova et al., 2006; Sigrist et al., 1995; Wolf et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies showing anaphase delays with non-degradable Cyclin B expression

claim: The anaphase delay caused by non-degradable B-type Cyclins is dependent on Cdk1 activity
source: While this delay was dependent on Cdk1 activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–e)
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that Cdk1 inhibition rescues the anaphase delay caused by non-degradable Cyclin B expression

claim: Proteasome inhibition with MG132 at anaphase onset causes cells to remain in an anaphase-like state for several hours with separated sister chromatids
source: As so, we also investigated the effect of inhibiting proteasome-mediated degradation of wild-type B-type Cyclins, including endogenously tagged versions, by adding MG132 just before or at anaphase onset in Drosophila and human cells, respectively. Under these conditions, cells remained in an anaphase-like state for several hours with separated sister chromatids and detectable Cyclin B1, often reverting to a metaphase-like state (Figure 3a,d,e, Figure 4a,d,e, Figure 6a,b,f and Videos 5 and 6).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data showing prolonged anaphase arrest with detectable Cyclin B1 after MG132 treatment in both Drosophila and human cells

claim: Aurora B inhibition in MG132-treated anaphase cells is not sufficient to drive cells out of mitosis
source: After Aurora B inhibition with Binucleine-2 (Smurnyy et al., 2010) or ZM447439 (Ditchfield et al., 2003) in Drosophila and human cells, respectively, they also remained in an anaphase-like state for several hours and often reverted into a metaphase-like state, but mitotic exit was resumed significantly earlier than MG132-treated controls (Figure 3b,d, Figure 4b,d,e and Videos 7 and 8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that Aurora B inhibition in MG132-arrested cells does not immediately trigger mitotic exit, though it occurs earlier than controls

claim: Cdk1 inhibition immediately triggers chromosome decondensation and mitotic exit in MG132-treated anaphase cells
source: In contrast, Cdk1 inhibition immediately triggered chromosome decondensation and mitotic exit (Figure 3c,d, Figure 4c–e and Videos 9 and 10).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing rapid mitotic exit after Cdk1 inhibition in MG132-arrested anaphase cells

claim: Cdk1 activity during anaphase is rate-limiting for mitotic exit in metazoans
source: Thus, Aurora B inhibition is clearly not sufficient to drive cells out of mitosis if Cyclin B1 degradation is prevented, whereas Cdk1 activity during anaphase is rate-limiting for mitotic exit in metazoans.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results showing that Cdk1 inhibition, but not Aurora B inhibition, immediately triggers mitotic exit in MG132-arrested cells

claim: Drosophila Cyclin B1 contains a KEN box at position 248
source: Sequence analysis of Drosophila Cyclin B1 revealed a KEN box at position 248, which we mutated to AAN (Figure 5a–d).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5

claim: The KEN-box mutant of Cyclin B1 is more slowly degraded specifically during anaphase
source: When expressed in S2 cells the KEN-Cyclin B1-GFP mutant was more slowly degraded specifically during anaphase, delaying mitotic exit (Figure 5a,b,d,f,g).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing increased Cyclin B1 half-life and delayed anaphase in KEN-box mutant expressing cells

claim: APC/CCdh1 depletion causes an accumulation of Cyclin B1 in Drosophila and human cells
source: In agreement, APC/CCdh1 depletion in Drosophila and human cells was previously shown to cause an accumulation of Cyclin B1 (Ma et al., 2012; Meghini et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating Cyclin B1 accumulation after Cdh1 depletion

claim: Fzr RNAi significantly delays Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase and postpones mitotic exit
source: To directly test whether APC/CCdh1 mediates Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase we performed RNAi against the Drosophila Cdh1 orthologue Fizzy-related (Fzr). As in the case of the KEN-box mutant, Fzr RNAi significantly delayed Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase, postponing mitotic exit (Figure 5e–j).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased Cyclin B1 half-life and delayed anaphase after Fzr depletion

claim: Combining KEN-box mutation with Apcin treatment at anaphase onset has a synergistic effect on Cyclin B1 degradation
source: Lastly, we combined our KEN-box mutant with acute APC/C inhibition at anaphase onset with the D-box competitor Apcin (Sackton et al., 2014) and found a synergistic effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing additive effects on Cyclin B1 half-life when combining KEN-box mutation with Apcin treatment

claim: Multiple recognition sites mediate Cyclin B1 degradation through both APC/CCdc20 and APC/CCdh1 during anaphase
source: This result suggests the presence of multiple recognition sites that mediate Cyclin B1 degradation through both APC/CCdc20 and APC/CCdh1 during anaphase.
evidence: Inference based on synergistic effects observed when combining KEN-box mutation with D-box inhibition

claim: Simultaneous addition of pro-TAME and Apcin at anaphase onset blocks continuous degradation of Cyclin B1 during anaphase in human cells
source: Only the simultaneous addition of both drugs at anaphase onset blocked the continuous degradation of Cyclin B1 during anaphase and prevented mitotic exit for several hours, similar to proteasome inhibition (Figure 6a–f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that combined APC/C inhibition with pro-TAME and Apcin prevents Cyclin B1 degradation and mitotic exit

claim: Drosophila and human Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase is mediated through the D-box and KEN-box (when present) by APC/CCdc20 or APC/CCdh1
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Drosophila and human Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase is mediated through the D-box and KEN-box (when present), and can be carried out either by APC/CCdc20 or APC/CCdh1.
evidence: Inference based on multiple experimental results including KEN-box mutation, Fzr depletion, and APC/C inhibitor studies

claim: Cyclin B1-GFP localizes at the spindle midzone and midbody during normal mitosis and cytokinesis in Drosophila S2 cells
source: To investigate the precise localization of Cyclin B1 during anaphase we took advantage of the extremely flat morphology of Drosophila S2 cells growing on concanavalin-coated coverslips. This allowed us to detect a faint pool of Cyclin B1-GFP associated with the spindle midzone and midbody during a normal mitosis and cytokinesis, respectively (Figure 7a,a', b), as reported previously in Drosophila germ cells (Mathieu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data showing Cyclin B1-GFP localization at the spindle midzone/midbody, consistent with previous reports

claim: Cyclin B1 co-localizes with Aurora B at the spindle midzone after Cdk1 inactivation during metaphase
source: Detection of the midzone pool of endogenous or ectopically expressed Cyclin B1 was enhanced by abrupt Cdk1 inactivation during metaphase, causing cells to prematurely enter anaphase with high Cyclin B1 levels (Figure 7c,e; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,b'). Under these conditions, Cyclin B1 co-localized with Aurora B at the spindle midzone (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing co-localization of Cyclin B1 and Aurora B at the midzone after Cdk1 inhibition

claim: Cyclin B1 localization at the spindle midzone depends on Subito/kinesin-6-mediated midzone targeting and Aurora B activity
source: This localization depended on Subito/kinesin-6-mediated midzone targeting and activity of Aurora B (Figure 7b,d,e), but was independent of Polo kinase activity (Figure 7g and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing loss of Cyclin B1 midzone localization after Subito depletion or Aurora B inhibition, but not after Polo inhibition

claim: Human Cdk1-GFP localizes to the spindle at the metaphase-anaphase transition and enriches in the central spindle region throughout anaphase
source: While we were unable to localize endogenously tagged Cyclin B1-Venus at the spindle midzone in human anaphase cells due to the poor signal/noise at this stage, direct localization of human Cdk1-GFP in live human HeLa cells revealed a clear spindle localization at the metaphase-anaphase transition, with a subsequent enrichment in the central spindle region between separating sister chromosomes throughout anaphase, and midbody during cytokinesis (Figure 7—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data showing Cdk1-GFP localization patterns during anaphase in human cells

claim: Cdk1 is enriched on isolated midbodies from human cells
source: In agreement, Cdk1 was recently found enriched on isolated midbodies from human cells (Capalbo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent study identifying Cdk1 on isolated midbodies

claim: Cyclin B1-Cdk1 is spatially regulated by Aurora B activity at the spindle midzone in Drosophila cells
source: These results suggest that Cyclin B1-Cdk1 is spatially regulated by Aurora B activity at the spindle midzone, at least in Drosophila cells.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing Aurora B-dependent localization of Cyclin B1 at the midzone

claim: Aurora B overexpression delays its own transition to the spindle midzone and extends anaphase duration
source: For this purpose we overexpressed Aurora B in Drosophila S2 cells and found that this delayed its own transition to the spindle midzone and extended anaphase duration (Figure 7—figure supplement 4a,b,d,e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing delayed Aurora B midzone localization and increased anaphase duration after Aurora B overexpression

claim: Aurora B association with the spindle midzone is a strong predictor of anaphase duration
source: Moreover, we found that Aurora B association with the spindle midzone is a strong predictor of anaphase duration, with several cells overexpressing Aurora B extending anaphase for more than 15 min (Figure 7—figure supplement 4c,e,f).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing strong relationship between Aurora B midzone localization timing and anaphase duration

claim: The anaphase delay caused by Aurora B overexpression depends on Cdk1 activity
source: Interestingly, this anaphase delay depended on Cdk1 activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 4c), suggesting that Aurora B association with the spindle midzone is able to delay mitotic exit by regulating Cdk1 activity during anaphase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that Cdk1 inhibition rescues the anaphase delay caused by Aurora B overexpression

claim: Subito/Mklp2/kinesin-6 RNAi causes a delay in Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase
source: To test this, we monitored Cyclin B1-GFP/Venus degradation after Subito/Mklp2/kinesin-6 RNAi in Drosophila S2 and human hTERT-RPE1 cells. This caused a short, but significant delay in Cyclin B1-GFP/Venus degradation during anaphase, increasing Cyclin B1 half-life and often delaying mitotic exit (Figure 8a–e; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–f).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing increased Cyclin B1 half-life and delayed anaphase after Subito/Mklp2 depletion

claim: The chromatin-targeted FRET biosensor specifically reports on elevated Cyclin B1-Cdk1 activity in mitosis relative to interphase
source: Importantly, there were statistically significant differences between the lifetime parameters of the chromatin-targeted phosphorylatable reporter in mitosis versus interphase, most notably the mean donor lifetime decreased from 3.43 ns + /- 0.12 ns (mean + /- S.D.) in interphase to 3.15 ns + /- 0.28 ns in mitosis (includes prophase, prometaphase, and metaphase cells) (Figure 9a, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements showing statistically significant differences in donor lifetime and FRET efficiency between interphase and mitosis

claim: The FRET biosensor is non-responsive to activities of Aurora B and Plk1
source: Importantly, the biosensor was shown to be highly specific for Cyclin B1-Cdk1 and non-responsive to activities of the midzone-enriched kinases Aurora B and Plk1 (Gavet and Pines, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous characterization of the biosensor specificity

claim: Lagging chromosomes in the vicinity of the spindle midzone exhibit higher Cdk1 activity than segregated chromosomes during anaphase
source: Remarkably, there was a statistically significant reduction in the donor lifetime (2.61 ns + /- 0.43 ns) for the sensor on lagging chromosomes in the vicinity of the spindle midzone compared to the donor lifetime (3.16 ns + /- 0.20 ns) on the segregated chromosomes (Figure 9a,b). This corresponds to ~3 fold increase in the FRET E of the sensor on lagging chromosomes (27.0% + /- 12.0%) relative to the FRET E of the reporter on segregated DNA (11.7% + /- 5.5%) (Figure 9a,c).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET measurements showing statistically significant differences in donor lifetime and FRET efficiency between lagging and segregated chromosomes

claim: There is a gradient of Cyclin B1-Cdk1 activity in the vicinity of the midzone during anaphase
source: The FLIM-FRET data support the conclusion that there is a gradient of CyclinB1-Cdk1 activity in the vicinity of the midzone during anaphase that locally phosphorylates chromatin bound substrates on incompletely separated chromosomes.
evidence: Inference based on FLIM-FRET measurements showing higher Cdk1 activity on lagging chromosomes near the midzone

claim: The Cdk1 activity gradient on lagging chromosomes is abolished by RO-3306 treatment
source: We argue that this activity gradient, which is reminiscent of a previously visualized midzone-based gradient of Aurora B kinase activity (Afonso et al., 2014; Fuller et al., 2008), specifically reports on midzone-proximal Cyclin B1-Cdk1 activity rather than that of other midzone-enriched kinases since the sensor is insensitive to inhibition of Aurora B or Plk1 activities (Gavet and Pines, 2010) and the activity gradient was no longer evident on lagging chromosomes/chromatin following addition of the Cdk1 inhibitor RO-3306 (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: Supported by FLIM-FRET data showing loss of activity gradient after Cdk1 inhibition, combined with previous characterization of biosensor specificity

claim: Aurora B mediates Cyclin B1 phosphorylation in Drosophila germline and human mitotic cells
source: Aurora B has been shown to mediate Cyclin B1 phosphorylation in Drosophila germline and human mitotic cells (Kettenbach et al., 2011; Mathieu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating Aurora B-mediated Cyclin B1 phosphorylation

claim: Inhibition of Aurora B activity at anaphase onset does not accelerate Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase
source: First, we monitored Cyclin B1-GFP/Venus levels after acute inhibition of Aurora B activity at anaphase onset by treating S2 and hTERT-RPE1 cells with Binucleine-2 or ZM447439, respectively. We found that inhibition of Aurora B activity did not accelerate Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase (Figure 10—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing no change in Cyclin B1 degradation kinetics after Aurora B inhibition at anaphase onset

claim: PP1/PP2A phosphatase activity is not required to regulate Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase
source: Likewise, acute PP1/PP2A phosphatase inhibition with okadaic acid at anaphase onset did not interfere with normal Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase (Figure 10—figure supplement 1c). These results are consistent with our previous experiments, which showed that Aurora B inhibition at anaphase onset did not accelerate mitotic exit in both Drosophila and human cells (Afonso et al., 2014). In addition, these data indicate that PP1/PP2A phosphatase activity is not required to regulate Cyclin B1 degradation, namely its centrosomal-associated pool, during anaphase.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no effect of okadaic acid on Cyclin B1 degradation kinetics during anaphase

claim: Slowing down chromosome separation with taxol delays Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase
source: To do so, we slowed down chromosome separation by allowing S2 cells to enter anaphase after a short exposure (less than 15 min) to 10 nM taxol or after depletion of the kinesin-13 KLP10A by RNAi (Afonso et al., 2014; Rogers et al., 2004). We found that, under both conditions, Cyclin B1-GFP degradation during anaphase was significantly delayed (Figure 10a–c,e–g), consistent with the previously reported delay in mitotic exit (Afonso et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing increased Cyclin B1 half-life after taxol treatment or KLP10A depletion

claim: The delay in Cyclin B1 degradation caused by slowed chromosome separation is dependent on Aurora B activity
source: To test whether the observed delay in Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase was dependent on Aurora B activity, we acutely inhibited Aurora B with Binucleine-2 specifically at anaphase onset in taxol-treated cells. We found that Aurora B inhibition fully restored normal Cyclin B1 degradation in cells with slower chromosome separation (Figure 10d,f,g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that Aurora B inhibition rescues the Cyclin B1 degradation delay in taxol-treated cells

claim: Short exposure to 10 nM taxol does not prevent normal Aurora B accumulation at the spindle midzone
source: Importantly, the short exposure of cells to 10 nM taxol did not prevent normal Aurora B accumulation at the spindle midzone (Figure 10—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing normal Aurora B midzone localization in taxol-treated cells

claim: Chromosome separation is linked to Aurora B-mediated control of Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase that licenses mitotic exit
source: Overall, these data link chromosome separation to Aurora B-mediated control of Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase that ultimately licenses mitotic exit.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results showing that slowing chromosome separation delays Cyclin B1 degradation in an Aurora B-dependent manner

claim: Degradation of B-type Cyclins specifically during anaphase is rate-limiting for mitotic exit in animals that diverged more than 900 million years ago
source: Taken together, our work reveals that degradation of B-type Cyclins specifically during anaphase is rate-limiting for mitotic exit among animals that diverged more than 900 million years ago.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data from Drosophila, mouse, and human cells showing conserved role of Cyclin B degradation during anaphase

claim: Cdk1 activity during anaphase is a function of chromosome separation and is spatially regulated by Aurora B localization and activity at the spindle midzone
source: Most importantly, we show that Cdk1 activity during anaphase is a function of chromosome separation and is spatially regulated by Aurora B localization and activity at the spindle midzone.
evidence: Inference based on multiple experimental results including FLIM-FRET measurements, Aurora B dependency experiments, and chromosome separation manipulation studies

claim: A crosstalk between molecular 'rulers' (Aurora B) and 'clocks' (B-type Cyclins-Cdk1) ensures that cells only exit mitosis after proper chromosome separation during anaphase
source: In concert with previous work (Afonso et al., 2014), our findings unveil an unexpected crosstalk between molecular 'rulers' (Aurora B) and 'clocks' (B-type Cyclins-Cdk1) that ensures that cells only exit mitosis after proper chromosome separation during anaphase, consistent with the previously proposed chromosome separation checkpoint hypothesis (Afonso et al., 2014; Maiato et al., 2015).
evidence: Inference based on integration of current experimental findings with previous work on Aurora B-mediated spatial control

claim: APC/CCdc20 mediates the initial degradation of Cyclin B1 during metaphase under SAC control
source: According to this model, APC/CCdc20 mediates the initial degradation of Cyclin B1 during metaphase under SAC control.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results and integration with established knowledge about SAC control of APC/CCdc20

claim: The decrease in Cdk1 activity as cells enter anaphase targets Aurora B to the spindle midzone via Subito/Mklp2/kinesin-6
source: The consequent decrease in Cdk1 activity as cells enter anaphase targets Aurora B to the spindle midzone (via Subito/Mklp2/kinesin-6)
evidence: Inference based on experimental results showing Aurora B midzone localization depends on Subito/Mklp2 and is negatively regulated by Cdk1

claim: Aurora B at the spindle midzone establishes a phosphorylation gradient that locally delays APC/CCdc20- and APC/CCdh1-mediated degradation of residual Cyclin B1 at the spindle midzone
source: Aurora B at the spindle midzone (counteracted by PP1/PP2A phosphatases on chromatin [Vagnarelli et al., 2011]) establishes a phosphorylation gradient that locally delays APC/CCdc20- and APC/CCdh1-mediated degradation of residual Cyclin B1 (and possibly B3) at the spindle midzone, at least in Drosophila cells.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results showing Aurora B-dependent delay in Cyclin B1 degradation and localization at the midzone

claim: As chromosomes separate and move away from the spindle midzone, Cdk1 activity decreases, allowing PP1/PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of Cdk1 and Aurora B substrates necessary for mitotic exit
source: Consequently, as chromosomes separate and move away from the spindle midzone, Cdk1 activity decreases, allowing the PP1/PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of Cdk1 and Aurora B substrates (e.g. Lamin B and Condensin I) necessary for mitotic exit.
evidence: Inference based on FLIM-FRET data showing Cdk1 activity gradient and experimental results linking chromosome position to Cyclin B1 degradation

claim: Cdk1 inactivation promotes the recruitment of PP1 phosphatase to chromosomes to locally oppose Aurora B phosphorylation
source: This model is consistent with the recent demonstration that Cdk1 inactivation promotes the recruitment of PP1 phosphatase to chromosomes to locally oppose Aurora B phosphorylation (Qian et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent study demonstrating PP1 recruitment after Cdk1 inactivation

claim: The model is consistent with equivalent phosphorylation and dephosphorylation events during mitotic exit in budding yeast
source: and recent findings in budding yeast demonstrating equivalent phosphorylation and dephosphorylation events during mitotic exit (Touati et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent findings in yeast showing similar regulatory mechanisms

claim: The model is consistent with premature Greatwall inactivation and PP2A:B55 reactivation predicted after acute Cdk1 inactivation during anaphase
source: It is also consistent with a premature Greatwall inactivation and PP2A:B55 reactivation that would be predicted after acute Cdk1 inactivation during anaphase (Cundell et al., 2013; Cundell et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference based on integration with previous work on Greatwall-PP2A:B55 regulation by Cdk1

claim: Cyclin B1 was degraded by the end of metaphase in human HeLa and rat kangaroo Ptk1 cells
source: Previous landmark work has carefully monitored the kinetics of Cyclin B1 degradation in living human HeLa and rat kangaroo Ptk1 cells during mitosis, and concluded that Cyclin B1 was degraded by the end of metaphase, becoming essentially undetectable as cells entered anaphase (Clute and Pines, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on Cyclin B1 degradation kinetics

claim: A small pool of Cyclin B1 continued to be degraded during anaphase in Ptk1 cells
source: However, we noticed that, consistent with our findings, a small pool of Cyclin B1 continued to be degraded during anaphase in Ptk1 cells (Clute and Pines, 1999).
evidence: Inference based on re-interpretation of data from a previous study

claim: Human DLD-1 cells undergoing normal mitosis entered anaphase with as much as 32% of Cyclin B1 compared to metaphase levels
source: Subsequent work investigating cellular response to anti-mitotic drugs has also shown that human DLD-1 cells undergoing normal mitosis entered anaphase with as much as 32% of Cyclin B1 compared to metaphase levels (Gascoigne and Taylor, 2008), suggesting that human cells enter anaphase with significant Cdk1 activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to a study showing substantial Cyclin B1 levels at anaphase onset

claim: Quantitative analysis with a FRET biosensor in human HeLa cells revealed residual Cdk1 activity during anaphase
source: Indeed, quantitative analysis with a FRET biosensor in human HeLa cells also revealed residual Cdk1 activity during anaphase (Gavet and Pines, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study using FRET biosensor to measure Cdk1 activity

claim: Expression of non-degradable Cyclin B1 during anaphase 'reactivates' the SAC, inhibiting APC/CCdc20
source: For example, it was shown that expression of non-degradable Cyclin B1 during anaphase 'reactivates' the SAC, inhibiting APC/CCdc20 (Clijsters et al., 2014; Rattani et al., 2014; Vázquez-Novelle et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing SAC reactivation by non-degradable Cyclin B1

claim: Human Cyclin B2 contains a recognizable KEN box
source: Interestingly, human Cyclin B2 (which contains a recognizable KEN box), as well as Cdk1, were identified at the midbody
evidence: Statement based on sequence analysis and previous characterization of human Cyclin B2

claim: Cdk1 inactivation during late mitosis is required for the timely completion of cytokinesis in human cells
source: and Cdk1 inactivation during late mitosis was required for the timely completion of cytokinesis in human cells (Capalbo et al., 2019; Mathieu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing requirement for Cdk1 inactivation during cytokinesis

claim: In human cells, Cdk1 activity during anaphase may be regulated not only by Cyclin B1, but also by Cyclin B2
source: Thus, it is possible that in human cells, Cdk1 activity during anaphase is regulated not only by Cyclin B1, but also by Cyclin B2.
evidence: Speculation based on the presence of Cyclin B2 at the midbody and its KEN box

claim: Direct Cyclin B1 phosphorylation by Aurora B may spatially regulate Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase
source: One possibility is that direct Cyclin B1 phosphorylation by Aurora B (Kettenbach et al., 2011; Mathieu et al., 2013) spatially regulates Cyclin B1 degradation during anaphase, mediated by both APC/CCdc20 and APC/CCdh1.
evidence: Speculation based on known Aurora B phosphorylation of Cyclin B1 and experimental results showing Aurora B-dependent regulation

claim: Aurora B may indirectly control Cyclin B1 during anaphase by regulating APC/CCdc20 and/or APC/CCdh1 activity
source: Another non-mutually exclusive possibility is that Aurora B indirectly controls Cyclin B1 during anaphase by regulating APC/CCdc20 and/or APC/CCdh1 activity, as recently shown for Cdk1 (Fujimitsu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation based on recent findings showing Cdk1 regulation of APC/C activity

claim: Mitotic exit is determined during anaphase and not at the metaphase-anaphase transition under SAC control
source: The main conceptual implication of these findings is that, contrary to what was previously assumed, mitotic exit is determined during anaphase and not at the metaphase-anaphase transition under SAC control.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results showing that Cdk1 activity during anaphase is rate-limiting for mitotic exit

claim: Mild induction of Cyclin B1-GFP expression in S2 cells reproduces the localization of endogenous Cyclin B1
source: Mild induction of Cyclin B1-GFP expression in S2 cells reproduced the localization of endogenous Cyclin B1 in the cytoplasm, mitotic spindle, kinetochores and centrosomes (Bentley et al., 2007; Clute and Pines, 1999; Huang and Raff, 1999; Pines and Hunter, 1991), without altering normal anaphase duration or increasing chromosome missegregation (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,a' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and quantification showing normal mitotic progression in cells expressing Cyclin B1-GFP, consistent with previous reports

claim: Aurora B association with the spindle midzone depends on kinesin-6/Mklp2/Subito
source: Interestingly, Aurora B association with the spindle midzone depends on the kinesin-6/Mklp2/Subito (Cesario et al., 2006; Gruneberg et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating kinesin-6 dependency of Aurora B midzone localization

claim: Aurora B association with the spindle midzone is negatively regulated by Cdk1
source: and is negatively regulated by Cdk1 (Hümmer and Mayer, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study showing Cdk1-mediated negative regulation of Aurora B midzone localization

claim: The establishment of a midzone-based Aurora B 'ruler' in anaphase is determined by the sudden drop of Cdk1 activity at the metaphase-anaphase transition
source: Thus, the establishment of a midzone-based Aurora B 'ruler' in anaphase is determined by the sudden drop of Cdk1 activity (the 'clock') at the metaphase-anaphase transition.
evidence: Inference based on the negative regulation of Aurora B midzone localization by Cdk1

claim: An Aurora B-dependent spatial control mechanism regulates normal nuclear envelope reformation in human cells
source: An Aurora B-dependent spatial control mechanism regulating normal NER in human cells has been recently confirmed (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent study confirming Aurora B-dependent spatial control of NER

claim: Nuclear envelope defects associated with incomplete chromosome separation during anaphase were proposed as an inevitable pathological condition
source: However, nuclear envelope defects associated with incomplete chromosome separation during anaphase (namely, anaphase lagging chromosomes due to mitotic errors) were proposed as an inevitable pathological condition.
evidence: Reference to interpretation from a previous study

claim: A molecular network operates during anaphase that promotes chromosome segregation fidelity by controlling mitotic exit in space and time
source: The present work provides yet additional evidence for a molecular network operating during anaphase that promotes chromosome segregation fidelity by controlling mitotic exit in space and time (Figure 11).
evidence: Inference based on integration of all experimental findings presented in the study
